topics.topic: Exact byte accounting for the multipart head, file, and closing delimiter
questions: Which raw bytes comprise the bounded head: only multipart-body bytes before the file content, or also HTTP request headers, the file part's headers, boundary bytes, and the CRLF adjoining the file content?

Exactly which bytes belong to the head and to the closing delimiter for this subtraction, including the CRLF before the final boundary, the final `--`, the trailing CRLF, and any permitted epilogue; and what happens when the request length is absent, invalid, or smaller than that overhead?
Which exact bytes belong to the file, the head and the closing delimiter, including the CRLF immediately before the closing boundary and the CRLF after it?

judgement.why: P3 already judges the same question about the exact multipart head, file-part delimiter, terminal bytes, epilogue, and declared-length subtraction, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Exact multipart framing subtracted to derive the declared file length
quotes:
`upload_framing.read_upload_head` reads the head alone,
  at most `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` (8192 bytes) — the boundary from the
  content type, the CSRF part, the file part's headers — and answers
  `UploadHead`: the CSRF value, the delimiter `\r\n--<boundary>` that ends
  the file part, and the file part's declared length — the request's
  declared length less the head read and the closing delimiter with its
  final `--\r\n` — or none of them.

The declared length `_read_bounded`
  compares is the file part's, so a file of exactly 50 MB is read (A19 rule
  4's required test); a body with an epilogue after the closing delimiter
  declares more than its file, and only a file that near the limit is then
  refused early. The bytes are counted over the file part as it is read.
precedent.why: The State 6 contract fixes the head, delimiter, terminal bytes, treatment of an epilogue, and the derived length used for the early size check.

topics.topic: Meaning and enforcement behavior of the multipart head limit
questions: What exactly must Registry do when the file part has not begun by `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`: refuse the upload, terminate the request, or handle the excess head another way?
What must Registry do when the bytes before the file would exceed `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`, and must it stop before reading the first excess byte or merely before reading file data?

Does the constant limit all pre-file bytes consumed, the largest buffer retained while parsing them, or only the canonical form head, and exactly what must Registry do when the limit is reached before the file begins?

judgement.why: P2 already judges what happens when the file part has not begun within the multipart-head bound, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Behavior when the file part has not begun at the multipart head limit
quotes:
Reads the stream up to the start of the file part's content and no further,
at most the bound; a head it refuses leaves the rest of the stream unread.
None: it reads the request's stream only.
precedent.why: The later upload-framing operation stops at the bound, refuses the head, leaves the remaining request unread, and changes no state, so an earlier upload remains kept.

topics.topic: Meaning and required disposal timing of multipart head data that is “never kept”
questions: What does “never kept” mean for the multipart head, for how long may its raw bytes exist, and which accepted decision requires their disposal?
What does “never kept” require for the multipart head: no durable storage, no owner-session storage, no logging, disposal immediately after CSRF validation, or no complete in-memory buffering at all?

What does “never kept” forbid: durable or session retention only, retention after upload processing, or even temporary buffering required while parsing and validating the CSRF part and multipart headers?

judgement.why: P5 already judges the permitted temporary parsing state and prohibited retention of the multipart head, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: What retention of the parsed multipart head is prohibited and when it must be discarded
quotes:
A13 rule 7: the CSRF value is taken from the form's body, never from a URL,
and is neither checked nor kept here — `owner_sessions` checks it at the
session check. A19 rule 4 stays `migration_import`'s: no byte of the file is
read here, and the file part's stream, a `MultipartFileBody` over the same
stream and that delimiter, gives the file's bytes only as its reader asks.
None: it reads the request's stream only.

`UploadBody`'s one implementation is
  `MultipartFileBody(stream, delimiter)`, `policy`, owned by
  `upload_framing`: it gives the file part's bytes and ends before the
  delimiter, holding in memory no more than the delimiter's length of
  look-ahead, so `_parse_export` still receives the bare JSON object.
precedent.why: The later texts prohibit retained upload-framing state, permit only bounded parsing and delimiter look-ahead, and assign no state impact to reading the head.

topics.topic: Accepted multipart part structure and rejection of malformed or unexpected parts
questions: Which nonconforming multipart requests are refused: a file first, a missing or duplicate CSRF part, duplicate file parts, extra parts, a non-final file part, or malformed boundaries; and at what point is each refused?

Is this only a description of the owner interface's canonical request, or an acceptance rule requiring exactly one CSRF part first, exactly one file part second and no later parts; how are duplicate, reordered, unknown or trailing parts handled?

judgement.why: P1 already judges accepted multipart part order, cardinality, extra parts, malformed structure, and content type, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Accepted multipart part order, cardinality, extra parts, and content type
quotes:
The CSRF value the first part carries, the delimiter that ends the file
part, and the file part's declared length — the request's declared length
less the head it read and the closing delimiter with its final `--` and line
end, or none when the request declared none; or that the head is not of that form — no multipart content type or
boundary, a first part that is not the CSRF field, no second part that is
the file — or is longer than the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`
constant, with none of these values.

a stream that fails or ends before its
declared length is refused as `file_unreadable`, replacing nothing kept and
changing nothing of the session but the instant of its last request, which
every request carrying it moves (A13 rule 2) — and an
unreadable or malformed one is refused with its kind alone.
precedent.why: The later public API requires the CSRF field first and file second, rejects any other head, and makes trailing additional parts produce a declared-length mismatch rather than an alternative accepted upload.

questions: What numeric byte value does `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` have?
What exact byte value does `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` have in this release?

judgement.why: P7 already judges the numeric multipart-head limit and the bytes counted toward it, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Multipart head-limit value and the bytes counted toward it
quotes:
`upload_framing.read_upload_head` reads the head alone,
  at most `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` (8192 bytes) — the boundary from the
  content type, the CSRF part, the file part's headers — and answers
  `UploadHead`: the CSRF value, the delimiter `\r\n--<boundary>` that ends
  the file part, and the file part's declared length — the request's
  declared length less the head read and the closing delimiter with its

precedent.why: The State 6 contract fixes the limit at 8192 bytes and enumerates the boundary, CSRF part, and file-part headers as the bounded head.

topics.topic: Definition of the request's declared length when Content-Length is absent or transfer coding is used
questions: What exactly is the request's declared length—an HTTP `Content-Length` value, a framework-provided decoded-body length or another value—and how is it represented when transfer coding is used or no single length exists?

topics.topic: Handling invalid, inconsistent, truncated, or negative declared upload lengths
questions: Besides the size check, what must happen when the declared request length is invalid, yields a negative file length, ends before the closing delimiter, or disagrees with the bytes actually delivered, and which of these cases count as an unreadable upload?

judgement.why: P6 already judges absent, invalid, inconsistent, and prematurely terminated declared lengths and their refusal behavior, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Meaning and handling of missing, invalid, or inconsistent declared request/file length
quotes:
The request's unread body stream, its content type and its declared length,
or that it declared none.

The CSRF value the first part carries, the delimiter that ends the file
part, and the file part's declared length — the request's declared length
less the head it read and the closing delimiter with its final `--` and line
end, or none when the request declared none; or that the head is not of that form — no multipart content type or
boundary, a first part that is not the CSRF field, no second part that is
the file — or is longer than the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`
constant, with none of these values.

a stream that fails or ends before its
declared length is refused as `file_unreadable`, replacing nothing kept and
changing nothing of the session but the instant of its last request, which
every request carrying it moves (A13 rule 2) — and an
unreadable or malformed one is refused with its kind alone.
The bytes are counted over the file part as it is read.
precedent.why: The later contracts distinguish an absent declaration from a present one, derive the file-part length from framing, refuse premature stream termination as unreadable, and still enforce the actual streamed-byte limit.

topics.topic: Required validation and rejection order before reading file bytes

judgement.why: P9 already judges that migration-closure rejection precedes and excludes CSRF, multipart-head, and file-size validation, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Precedence between migration-closure rejection and A19 upload validation
quotes:
The closure first and alone: when it exists, `import_closed` is the answer,
before any other check (A16 rule 8; Conventions, "Stages").
precedent.why: The later import operation expressly checks the closure first and returns import_closed alone before validating or reading the upload.
